Measured on this build: the shade does NOT follow the vote. It stays at 120. The call is accepted, but the panel takes its mode from the foreground app\'s window, and SystemUI\'s shade, quick settings and lock screen are system overlays with no activity in that stack, so nothing ever reads the override.\n\nThe switch is kept for builds that behave differently. Where such a vote does land it pins the display rather than one app, and holds the lock screen and always-on display there too. Arm all always skips this row.
A rootless per-app refresh-rate unlock for the OnePlus 15 on OxygenOS 16. What it does to your phone, in short pieces.
Pins a refresh rate on the apps you choose: 60, 90, 120, 144 or 165 Hz. Pick the rate at the top, then tap an app to arm it at that rate. Tap the row details for a rate that app alone should use.
Arm all sweeps the whole list. Re-arm re-sends the saved set. Clear withdraws everything. The armed set survives reboots.

OxygenOS carries a display service whose requestGameRefreshRate call has no permission check on the caller, so any app can ask for a rate on behalf of any package. It is the same request the system game mode uses, which is why no root is needed.
The vendor rate ids are not in Hz order: id 1 is 90 Hz and id 2 is 60 Hz. An early build read them the other way round, so those two rates ran at the one you had not picked.
The request sets the panel minimum and maximum to the same rate. While an armed app is on screen the panel has no range left to move inside, so it is a pin rather than a ceiling.
What each rate can idle to
Every rate selects a panel mode with its own idle floor. Measured on this build: 165 rests at 55 Hz, 144 near 48, 60 and 90 at 30, and 120 goes all the way down to 1.

Game engines re-pin their own frame rate whenever they take focus, which overwrites a one-shot request. The watchdog re-issues the vote while the screen is on so ours lands last. Its notification says how many apps it is holding.
Why the app on screen decides the order

The system writes the request onto the windows of the package it names, and the panel follows whichever write landed last. So every pass ends on the app you are using. A pass ending on a background app would vote for windows that do not exist and drop the pin it had just set.

When nothing on screen is moving, the vote is swapped for 120, the one rate whose mode spans 1 to 120. The panel can then ramp down while the vote itself stays held. Content that needs more than 120 gets the armed rate back in about 55 ms.

Only 144, and that is a measurement rather than a rule. From 144 the switch to 120 is clean and the panel ramps to 1 Hz. From 165 it lands on a pinned 120, higher than the 55 Hz that mode idles to on its own, so parking it would cost power. A still 165 screen rests at 55 Hz and that is the floor here. 120 already is the park, and 60 or 90 are ceilings you picked to keep faster content off the panel.

The shade, quick settings and lock screen belong to SystemUI, not to the app you are in. Arming it does nothing on this build: the panel takes its mode from the foreground app window, and those are overlays. The row stays for builds that behave differently, and Arm all always skips it.

That one does work, and doubles as a self test. If this app\'s own screen will not reach the rate you armed it at, no vote is landing at all. The smoothness test has its own switch for the same thing, and that one gives the hold back when you leave the page. Arm all skips both rows.

The smoothness test draws one lane of moving blocks per rate, each allowed to update only at its own rate. The lane matching the panel glides and the slower ones step. The readout is the panel measured from its own frame timing, and the marker colour is yours to pick: which colour shows a moving edge best is a property of the screen, not of the test.

Disarm withdraws the vote by asking for rate id 0, the vendor cancel. Sending the rate again would only write the same pin back. A reboot clears every vote, because the vendor keeps them in memory only.

The permanent per-app override is permission protected and closed to a rootless app, so a vote applies only while its app is in the foreground. Video can judder when forced above its own cadence: pin those at 60 or leave them unarmed. Battery and heat rise with the rate and with the number of armed apps.
An OTA can close the hole at any time. A SecurityException in the log is what that looks like.

Settings has a Live log page. Arm165 lines are this app: vote results, the app it sees on screen, parks and restores. RefreshRate lines are the vendor framework. Share sends the buffer for a bug report.
